newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: SOCCER-FIFA REJECT CELTIC'S COMPENSATION CLAIM.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-FIFA REJECT CELTIC'S COMPENSATION CLAIM.

text.p: Glasgow Celtic's claim for two million pounds ($3.3 million) compensation from AS Monaco for Scottish international John Collins was rejected by FIFA, world soccer's governing body, on Friday.

Celtic claimed that a fee was due for the player, who moved on a free transfer to Monaco in July, because the club is outside the European Union, despite being a member of the French Football Federation (FFF).

Celtic said that Monaco were not entitled to rely on the Bosman ruling which allows players to move without a fee between member states of the EU when a player has finished his contract, as Collins had done.
But FIFA's player status committee ruled that Moncao had no alternative but to belong to the FFF because the principality of Monaco does not have its own national association.

A statement said: "...the transfer took place between two clubs of national associations both located in EU territory and according to the ruling of the EU court in the so-called Bosman case, no compensation is due."

Celtic had argued that as Monaco has a separate government structure and an independent tax system it cannot be viewed as part of France. They may now consider taking the case to court in Switzerland where both FIFA and UEFA are based.
Ironically, Collins said only last week he was disappointed that he was only playing in front of just 3,000 to 4,000 fans a week at Monaco and he missed the big crowds in Scotland.
But there was better news for Celtic and Alan Stubbs who joined them from Bolton earlier this year.
Celtic and Stubbs had earlier been heavily fined by FIFA because an unlicensed agent was involved in his transfer.
Celtic were told in August they could not appeal, but the status committee ruled on Friday that because of a legal loophole, the club could now appeal.

In another ruling, the committee rejected France's request to have their players released by clubs five days instead of two days before friendlies in the run-up to the World Cup finals which the French host in 1998.
